tip: 'Sekali' after its word means 'very': 'deras sekali' = very hard. In front it means 'once' instead ('sekali seminggu' = once a week) – position decides.
'Jam lima' = five o'clock, but flip it and 'lima jam' = five hours. Dad leaves at 'jam lima' – word order alone separates clock time from duration.
'Soalnya' = spoken 'because', after the statement: 'soalnya sudah malam' = because it's late. In writing: 'karena'.
'Ke-...-an' can mark something that happened by accident: 'dompetku ketinggalan' = my wallet got left behind, no one did it on purpose. Also 'kehujanan' = got rained on.
'Jadi' = so; it starts the result: 'hujan deras, jadi kami menunggu' = it rained hard, so we waited.
Doubling slows it down: 'pelan-pelan' = slowly, 'sarapan pelan-pelan' = a leisurely breakfast.
'-nya' can do the job of 'the': 'kopinya sudah habis' = the coffee is gone – the one you both know about. Indonesian has no separate word for 'the'.
This 'jadi' = 'so'; 'jadi' also means 'become' ('jadi guru' = become a teacher) – context decides.
'Supaya' = so that (a goal): 'supaya tidak lupa' = so that I don't forget. No extra word for 'that'.
Doubled adjective = 'into pieces that size': 'memotong buah kecil-kecil' = cut the fruit into small pieces.
'Agar' = 'supaya' in formal settings (announcements, notices): 'agar acara mulai tepat waktu'. Say 'supaya' in chat.
'Tetap' = still/anyway after 'meskipun': 'meskipun hujan, tetap berjalan' = although it rained, it still went ahead.
'Masih' = still ongoing: 'masih buka' = still open. 'Tetap' also translates 'still' but means 'anyway, regardless' – 'tetap buka' = stays open no matter what.
No 'tapi' needed after a 'meskipun' clause: 'meskipun jauh, dia datang' – not 'tapi dia datang'.
'Walaupun' and 'meskipun' both mean 'although' – swap freely: 'walaupun tua' = 'meskipun tua' = although (he's) old.
'-nya' glued to the end of a verb means 'it': 'menghabiskannya' = finished it. The object attaches straight onto the verb – no separate word for 'it' needed.
'Tetapi' = 'but' in careful or written style; in everyday talk say 'tapi': 'mahal, tapi enak' = pricey, but tasty.
'Ter-' here means it just happened, no doer in view: 'tertunda' = got delayed. 'Di-' points at a doer: 'ditunda' = was postponed by someone.
'Belum ... juga' = STILL not: 'belum datang juga' = still hasn't come (with impatience).
'Tinggal' here = left/remaining: 'warnanya tinggal hitam' = the only color left is black.
'Sambil' = while (one person, two actions at once): 'mendengarkan radio sambil menyetir' = listen while driving.
'Di-' = 'gets ...-ed': 'dipanggil' = gets called, 'namamu dipanggil' = your name is called.
No tense word needed after 'sebelum': 'sebelum anak-anak bangun' covers 'before the kids wake / woke up'.
'Ya' at the end softens a request: 'angkat jemuran, ya' = bring in the laundry, okay?
'Sesudah' = after; 'setelah' means the same: 'sesudah hujan berhenti' = after the rain stopped.
'Kalau tidak' = otherwise (literally 'if not'): 'kalau tidak, kita ketinggalan kereta' = otherwise we miss the train.
'Ke-...-an' can mean badly affected by: 'kedinginan' = freezing cold, 'kehujanan' = caught in the rain.
'Tawar-menawar' = haggling (back-and-forth doubling): 'bisa tawar-menawar' = you can bargain.
'Dia bilang dia akan datang' – 'bilang' connects straight to what was said, no word for 'that' required. Indonesian happily skips the connector English leans on.
After 'bilang', keep the original tense: 'ibu bilang makan malam sudah siap' – 'dinner is ready', not 'was ready'. Indonesian reports the words as they were spoken.
